body.text: Malaysia’s decision to restrict the use of Waze among civil servants raises concerns beyond the Israeli origins of a navigation application (app) that provides real-time traffic updates and route guidance. Waze grew out of FreeMap Israel, a crowdsourced mapping project established in 2006, and was acquired by Google in 2013 for USD969 million, according to Google’s financial filing. How should nation-states manage the potential security risks of everyday digital services that collect detailed movement data of their citizens, particularly when the service operators are abroad and foreign laws govern the terms of use? For Malaysia, which has never recognised the state of Israel and does not have diplomatic relations with it, the question is especially pertinent.

On 20 October 2026, Chief Secretary to the Government Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar issued a directive restricting civil servants’ use of Waze, following a decision by the National Cyber Security Committee (NCSC), which Prime Minister (PM) Anwar Ibrahim chairs. The Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) subsequently framed the restriction against Waze as a measure to protect government information and personal data from potential misuse by Israel. While the NCSC endorsed the ban, its abrupt rollout produced conflicting guidance. For instance, the relevant ‘frequently asked questions’ (FAQ) published by the National Cyber Security Agency (NACSA) says the ban applies during official duties (in its Introduction), yet elsewhere in the FAQ extends it to cover private journeys made outside working hours. Separately, PM Anwar urged the wider public to stop using Waze and consider Malaysian alternatives.

The jurisdictional concern is not unfounded. Google acquired Waze in 2013, but Waze’s data controller, Waze Mobile Ltd, is incorporated in Israel. Israeli law governs Waze’s terms of use and the terms designate Tel Aviv courts as having exclusive jurisdiction over service-related disputes, while Waze’s privacy policy describes the collection of GPS coordinates, time-stamped route histories, device information and, depending on user settings, user location data even when the application is not actively used. The terms permit disclosures (of such data) when legally required.

While such location data collection is not unique to Waze, there is still a need for consistent scrutiny of navigation applications. Why does this matter? Civil servants’ and political appointees’ location histories can reveal what regular journeys they make to government buildings, diplomatic premises, security facilities or private residences. A peer-reviewed study of mobility records showed how distinctive individual location traces can be, even when users’ identifying details are removed.

Israel’s documented use of surveillance technologies to monitor Palestinians, including practices investigated by Amnesty International, possibly provides the geopolitical context for Malaysia’s concerns. However, these investigations do not implicate Waze and there is no publicly substantiated evidence that Malaysian Waze users’ data have been shared with Israeli authorities. Still, the Malaysian government can and should assess any security exposure before a breach or disclosure occurs. For Malaysian cybersecurity authorities, the key questions would be: who can access location data under foreign laws, how long data is retained and how (and if) foreign data providers can be held accountable across jurisdictions.

Distinguishing identifiable risk from proven misuse requires a consistent policy response. However, while Malaysia’s Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) 2010 regulates the collection, use and storage of personal data in commercial transactions, its requirements do not apply to federal and state governments. The Cyber Security Act (CSA) 2024 addresses national cybersecurity governance and critical information infrastructure, while the Data Sharing Act 2025 governs specified federal public-sector data sharing. Yet these laws do not collectively establish a consistent procedure for assessing and approving commercial navigation apps for government use.

What is more, Malaysia’s Cyber Security (Exemption) Order 2025, P.U. (A) 47 exempted nine named corporate entities, including three Google entities and companies associated with Amazon and Microsoft, from all provisions of the CSA 2024, effective 1 February 2025. This order was questioned in Parliament on 14 October 2026. While Waze Mobile Ltd was not among those exempted, the exemptions raise questions about how well Malaysia balances investment incentives against cybersecurity safeguards. The government has cited investment and employment considerations and maintained that other Malaysian laws apply, but should clarify which cybersecurity safeguards cover the exempted entities and establish a timetable for reviewing whether the exemptions remain justified.
Digital sovereignty cannot be achieved simply by replacing dependence on foreign applications with inadequate domestic solutions.

Sensitive official journeys require clear controls, enforceable public-sector data safeguards and independent oversight. Ideally, Malaysia should develop a public-sector geolocation security framework coordinated by NACSA and the National Digital Department. Approval for official use should depend on independent assessments of data collection, retention, encryption, cross-border processing, foreign jurisdiction and third-party access.

The same scrutiny should extend to alternative apps recommended to Malaysians. The government’s promotion of TuJu, developed through a partnership involving the Malaysian Highway Authority (LLM) and Prosignal Consortium, provides an opening for domestic technological development, but some Malaysians have questioned its data permissions and usability. Notably, LLM apologised for technical disruptions on 22 October 2026. Former LLM chairman Abdul Rashid Asari admitted to inviting Prosignal without an open tender, following board approval. By 3 November 2026, TuJu’s Android app was redirecting users to Google Maps.

These concerns warrant transparent assessments and improvements but should not distract from the original concerns surrounding Waze. TuJu’s reported use of Google mapping data at launch illustrates why local development does not necessarily mean full control over the technology behind an app.

These developments present an opportunity for Malaysia’s technology sector. Rather than concentrating support on a single government-backed app, authorities could encourage private developers, startups, universities and local technology firms to build competing navigation services. Government agencies could provide developers with secure access to non-personal traffic, roadwork and highway data, alongside competitive grants and pilot programmes, while developers can compete on accuracy, road safety, accessibility, privacy and reliability. All apps need to meet the same independently established security standards before public release.

Malaysia’s decision to curtail its civil servants’ use of Waze brings the question of foreign jurisdiction over mobility data into its national security policy. Anwar’s appeal to the wider public reflects similar concerns about the potential misuse of ordinary Malaysians’ personal and movement data. The broader challenge is for the country to establish consistent safeguards for sensitive location data across digital services. Domestic alternatives will earn public trust only if they are competently developed, rigorously tested and reliable. Digital sovereignty cannot be achieved simply by replacing dependence on foreign applications with inadequate domestic solutions.
